strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical relevance: identifies genuine limitation that global geometric metrics fail to predict compositional binding despite their widespread use in representation learning

Rigorous experimental design with careful controls: synthetic task deliberately isolated to compositional binding, disjoint colors prevent shortcuts, comprehensive robustness analysis across metric formulations, neighborhood sizes, architectural covariates, and random seeds

Strong and consistent empirical findings: near-zero correlation for geometric metrics (r≈0.18, p>0.4) is robust across variations; JER shows strong predictive power (r=0.65, p=0.001); bivariate model explains 74% of variance with good cross-validation generalization (LOO-CV R²=0.65)

Comprehensive model coverage spanning 8 objective families (variance-decorrelation, contrastive, masked, vision-language, self-distillation, clustering, supervised): 21 models with different architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-S/B/L) enable generalizable conclusions about objective design

Theoretical grounding explaining empirical findings: Section 6 provides mechanistic account of how different training objectives expose different Jacobian functionals, with detailed derivations showing variance-decorrelation explicitly constrains second-order Jacobian statistics while others constrain projections

Excellent reproducibility infrastructure: extensive appendices with full implementation details, hyperparameters for all metrics, model sources/checkpoints, data generation procedures, statistical methodology clearly specified, multiple seed runs demonstrating stability

Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Figures 3-4 clearly demonstrate Jacobian rank collapse mechanisms; Figure 6 qualitative analysis shows concrete failure modes; writing is accessible and logical progression
weaknesses: Critically limited task scope severely restricts generalizability: only binary compositional binding (shape-position) on 3 simple shapes and 6 colors; no evaluation on complex relational structures, multi-attribute bindings, natural image compositions, or established benchmarks; unclear whether findings extend beyond this extremely minimal synthetic setting

Fundamental ecological validity concern with Jacobian measurement approach: JER computed on random noise (x ~ N(0.45, 0.225²)) but used to predict binding performance on synthetic shapes; no analysis of whether Jacobian structure on natural images differs significantly from noise; unjustified assumption that noise-based sensitivity predicts compositional understanding

Correlation interpreted as mechanistic insight without causal evidence: no experiments training models with JER regularization; no ablations manipulating JER during training; alternative explanations not explored; claims about 'critical complementary axis' exceed what correlation analysis supports

Theoretical analysis based on limiting assumptions with gaps to practical regime: first-order Taylor expansion assumes small perturbations around point; assumptions (isotropic augmentation perturbations Σ_δ ≈ σ²I) may not hold for realistic augmentations; doesn't rigorously prove why variance-decorrelation specifically achieves higher JER; first-order local analysis doesn't necessarily characterize global compositional behavior

No validation that findings matter for real tasks: all conclusions rest exclusively on synthetic binding performance; no evidence models with higher JER perform better on genuine compositional generalization tasks; unclear whether this synthetic capability translates to downstream applications or natural image understanding

Narrowly scoped geometric analysis: only 3 geometric metrics tested (Global PR, Global Isotropy, Local Isotropy); no ablation on metric definitions, alternative formulations, or combinations; no exploration of more sophisticated geometric approaches; negative result on geometry is somewhat limited in scope

Small sample size with potential overfitting: n=21 models is modest for correlation analysis (though jackknife helps); substantial gap between training and cross-validated R² (0.74 vs 0.65) suggests potential overfitting; vulnerability to outliers not fully addressed

Weak control using Same/Different discrimination: while Appendix E provides formal justification, Same/Different remains insufficient proxy; substantial variance in binding driven by discriminability (most models 50-75%); decomposition not fully convincing; potential task-specific shortcuts could inflate apparent discriminability

strengths: Identifies important disconnect between standard geometric metrics (isotropy, participation ratio) and compositional binding, challenging implicit assumptions in representation learning

Comprehensive evaluation across 21 encoders spanning multiple training objectives (contrastive, variance-decorrelation, masked prediction, vision-language, supervised) with thorough robustness analysis (seed stability, architectural controls, metric variations)
Well-designed synthetic benchmark isolating compositional binding via disjoint color constraint that prevents reliance on color co-occurrence, reducing confounds
Strong empirical finding: Jacobian Effective Rank (JER) achieves r=0.65 (p=0.001) vs. r=0.18 for isotropy, with bivariate model reaching R²=0.74 (LOO-CV 0.65)
Provides intuitive theoretical perspective explaining why variance-decorrelation objectives directly expose second-order Jacobian interactions while contrastive objectives constrain only projections
Extensive reproducibility details with comprehensive appendices covering hyperparameters, experimental procedures, and mathematical derivations
Qualitative analysis (Figure 6) effectively illustrates failure modes where models assign high similarity to both correct and incorrect structure-wise distractors
weaknesses: Critical scope limitation: Evaluation restricted to extremely minimal synthetic task (3 shapes, 6 colors, 2 positions) testing only shape-position bindings. No evidence that superior JER-predicted models transfer to natural-image compositional reasoning, standard compositionality benchmarks, or downstream transfer tasks—the core claim about 'compositional representation learning' is unsupported

Methodological concern: JER computed on random Gaussian noise (µ=0.45, σ²=0.225²) claimed to be 'decoupled from natural-image semantics' but lacks ablations showing this choice doesn't affect conclusions; no comparison with JER computed on natural/augmented images

Disjoint-color constraint may artificially penalize models learning realistic color-shape associations; this design choice plausibly favors variance-decorrelation objectives by construction, particularly explaining poor CLIP/vision-language performance which optimize for semantic-visual alignment

Theoretical analysis lacks rigor: Claim that objectives constrain only Jacobian components in ∂L/∂z (Eq. 4) is stated informally without proof; analysis is first-order/local but connection to global binding performance is assumed rather than derived; causality unclear—does high JER cause binding success or both emerge from objective design independently

Same/Different control paradoxically used as validating metric despite Appendix E proving it's insufficient for binding (permutation-invariant encoders achieve perfect performance); combining JER + Same/Different appears post-hoc rather than principled

Missing core validation: No evaluation on established compositional generalization benchmarks, no correlation with standard downstream transfer task performance, no cross-task validation that JER predicts other relational reasoning forms

Limited readout analysis: Only tests cosine similarity, kNN, and local PCA; conclusion that 'binding information is not concentrated locally' may be premature without stronger decoders or learned classifiers

No causal evidence: Shows correlation not causation; lacks intervention experiments (e.g., training models to maximize JER while controlling other factors) that would demonstrate whether JER improvements actually improve binding

Unclear practical implications: Primarily diagnostic without proposed training objectives or methods to improve compositional binding; actionability for practitioners is minimal—amounts to noting that variance-decorrelation objectives happen to perform better on this specific synthetic task

Presentation-scope mismatch: Title and introduction suggest broad claims about 'compositional representation learning' and 'representational competence' but evaluation is extremely narrow; oversells generality of findings

strengths: Clear and robust negative result: geometric metrics show near-zero correlation with compositional binding across multiple metrics and hyperparameter settings, challenging a foundational assumption in representation learning

Novel functional sensitivity diagnostic: Jacobian Effective Rank strongly predicts binding capability (r=0.65, p=0.001) and explains 74% of variance when combined with discriminability, offering a useful complementary evaluation metric
Comprehensive experimental scope: 21 encoders spanning 8 objective families, multiple architectures and scales, with controlled analysis isolating objective effects from architectural confounds

Well-designed synthetic task: Attribute binding task cleverly uses disjoint colors to force compositional reasoning and prevent feature co-occurrence shortcuts; control task appropriately contextualizes results

Mechanistic explanation: Section 6 provides intuitive account of how different objectives constrain different components of the Jacobian, explaining why global geometry and compositional capacity remain orthogonal

Excellent reproducibility: Complete implementation details, publicly available models, hyperparameter specifications, stability analysis across seeds (CV<2%), promised code release, and robustness checks for architectural covariates

Clear presentation: Effective figures (especially Figures 1, 3-4, 6) clearly communicate findings; qualitative analysis showing high similarity to both correct and incorrect structures is particularly persuasive

Honest treatment of limitations: Explicitly acknowledges scope limitations in Appendix A.1; clarifies that findings reflect objective-representation alignment rather than absolute claims about recoverability
weaknesses: Limited generalization: Evaluation restricted to synthetic tasks with simple primitives (3 shapes, 6 colors, binary spatial relations), raising questions about transfer to natural image compositional understanding or other compositional phenomena like hierarchical structure or counting

Jacobian computed on unstructured noise: JER measured on random Gaussian inputs rather than structured compositional perturbations; while this avoids dataset bias, the connection between noise sensitivity and compositional reasoning needs stronger justification

Causal claims not established: Paper correlates JER with binding but doesn't prove JER enables binding or rule out confounders; no interventions manipulating JER during training to validate causal mechanism

Modest sample size: Correlation analysis uses only n=21 models; leave-one-out analysis shows 19/21 retain p<0.05, but 2 outliers can affect significance at this scale; no multiple comparisons correction across tested metrics

Theoretical analysis lacks rigor: Section 6 is intuitive but informal; claim that objectives constrain 'only those components' in ∂L/∂z oversimplifies indirect effects through optimization dynamics; first-order expansion may miss nonlinearities; why effective rank is the right statistic lacks formal justification

Domain mismatch in metric computation: Geometric statistics computed on ImageNet-1k while binding evaluated on synthetic images; unclear if weak correlation persists when computing geometry on the synthetic task itself

Unclear practical implications: Paper identifies problem but proposes no solutions for improving compositional binding during training; lacks guidance on objective design or demonstration that maximizing JER improves real compositional capabilities

Incomplete explanation of failure modes: Vision-language models show JER≈19 (moderate rank) but near-chance binding; why doesn't high JER + reasonable discriminability suffice? Semantic axis explanation not empirically validated

strengths: Identifies important empirical disconnect: geometric metrics (isotropy, participation ratio) exhibit near-zero correlation with compositional binding while JER shows strong correlation (r=0.69, p<0.0001), challenging prevailing assumptions in representation learning

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 26 encoders spanning 7 objective families with multiple robustness checks: geometric metrics tested on different neighborhood sizes (k={8,16,32}), JER null-calibrated against random initialization, and natural-image validation on SugarCrepe (r=0.69 for CLIP variants)

Careful experimental design: synthetic binding task uses disjoint color sets between query/target to isolate compositional structure from appearance matching; Same/Different control properly disambiguates confounds from true binding capability

Mechanistic theoretical analysis connecting objective design to Jacobian structure: first-order analysis explains how variance-decorrelation objectives expose J(x) through second-order statistics while other objectives constrain only specific functional projections (Section 6, Equations 5-14)

Layer-wise analysis reveals where functional rank collapses: Barlow Twins maintains high rank throughout network; CLIP/DINOv2 show mid-network collapse; MAE collapses only at projection layer (Figure 4), providing insight into objective-specific mechanisms
Strong reproducibility practices: extensive appendix with hyperparameters (Tables 13-15), all models from public checkpoints (Table 12), wall-clock costs documented (Table 9), code release promised
Demonstrates complementary predictive power: JER + Discriminability combined explain 78% variance (LOO-CV R²=0.71), suggesting multiple independent factors contribute to compositional capability
weaknesses: No causal evidence: only shows correlation between JER and binding; no interventional experiments (e.g., training with JER regularizer) or ablation studies to establish that improving JER causally improves binding; remaining 22% unexplained variance suggests other unmeasured factors

Narrow compositional binding definition: synthetic task uses only 3 shapes, 6 colors, 2 positions (minimal complexity); primary evaluation on 500 trials with 4-way choice; SugarCrepe validation limited to 7 subtypes and only CLIP family (n=13), leaving unclear whether JER predicts other compositional forms (part-whole relations, structured reasoning beyond spatial bindings)

Small sample size statistical limitations: n=26 correlations have wide confidence intervals; some objective families have only 2-3 models limiting family-level claims; LOO-CV doesn't account for data-driven choice to combine JER+Discriminability; partial correlations may conflate mediation with confounding

Theoretical analysis uses first-order approximations assuming isotropic perturbation covariance (Σδ≈σ²I) which may not hold; doesn't rigorously explain why JER specifically (vs. other Jacobian properties like condition number) predicts binding; theoretical predictions (Section 6) not empirically validated on held-out test cases

Jacobian estimation via random projection introduces unquantified approximation error; natural-image JER (r=0.69) vs. Gaussian-noise JER (r=0.62) shows ~10% degradation, raising questions about claimed stimulus-agnosticism and whether off-manifold behavior reflects on-manifold properties

Missing key ablations: no comparison to alternative functional sensitivity measures (gradient norms, curvature, condition number); no learned-readout experiments to test whether binding information exists but requires nonlinear access; no experiments training with JER-regularization to validate causal impact

Limited generalization evidence: unclear if JER predicts performance on naturalistic compositional tasks, multi-object reasoning, or downstream applications; how JER relates to tasks where geometry IS predictive (classification, retrieval) unexplored; results may not generalize beyond vision domain or this specific binding definition

Presentation issues: title claim 'Global Geometry Is Not Enough' overstates findings since geometry remains informative for classification; Same/Different and Binding not fully independent (Section J correctly notes Same/Different is necessary but insufficient), so combining them (R²=0.78) may conflate correlated aspects rather than demonstrate independence

strengths: Identifies genuine empirical gap: geometric metrics (r≈0.1) fail to predict compositional binding, challenging industry-wide assumptions about representation quality
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 26 models across diverse objectives with extensive robustness checks for metric definitions, hyperparameters, and architectural covariates
Well-designed synthetic benchmark: attribute-binding task cleverly isolates compositional binding using disjoint color sets to eliminate feature-based shortcuts
Novel diagnostic metric: Jacobian Effective Rank (JER) shows strong correlation with binding (r=0.69, p<0.001), suggesting functional sensitivity matters for composition
Mechanistic analysis: Section 6 provides clear derivations showing how different objectives expose different Jacobian functionals, explaining objective-dependent JER variations
Thorough documentation: extensive appendices with implementation details, derivations, and supplementary robustness analyses support reproducibility
Qualitative failure mode analysis: Figure 6 effectively illustrates that models assign high similarity to both correct and incorrect bindings despite structural differences
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: evaluates only shape-position binding on minimal synthetic data (3 shapes, 6 colors); lacks tests for other compositional phenomena (color-shape, spatial relations) or visual complexity present in real binding problems

Weak mechanistic explanation: while paper shows JER correlates with binding and objectives constrain Jacobians differently, it does not explain WHY distributed input-output sensitivity should theoretically enable binding
Insufficient natural image validation: SugarCrepe evaluation limited to CLIP variants (n=13) rather than full 26-model suite, raising generalizability concerns across objective families
Expensive functional metric: JER requires 5-10 minutes per model vs. 2-5 seconds for geometric metrics, limiting practical utility for model selection and monitoring
Missing actionable insights: paper is purely diagnostic—identifies that geometry fails but provides no concrete objective modifications or training strategies to improve compositional binding
Unclear practical importance: CLIP and similar vision-language models show poor binding on synthetic tasks yet excel at downstream vision tasks, leaving motivation for practitioners unclear
Incomplete causal understanding: JER + discriminability explains R²=0.78 (LOO-CV: 0.71) leaving 22% of binding variance unexplained; missing factors not identified
Statistical limitations: n=26 models with unbalanced objective families (only 1 contrastive, 1 supervised classification model); no multiple-comparison correction; overfitting evident in LOO-CV

Insufficient metric justification: why participation ratio on Jacobian singular values rather than other Jacobian properties (spectral gap, condition number, Lipschitz constants)? Why only 32 random directions and 100 images?
No downstream task validation: paper never demonstrates that improving JER on synthetic binding tasks transfers to better real-world vision performance

Task validity questions: abstract shape-position binding may not capture 'compositional binding' as manifested in natural images with clutter, occlusion, and semantic features; no human baseline or task difficulty assessment

strengths: Identifies an important and non-obvious gap between global embedding geometry and compositional binding capability; challenges a widespread assumption in representation learning

Exceptionally thorough experimental design: 26 vision encoders across 6+ objective families, multiple architectural controls, extensive robustness checks (neighborhood sizes, metric formulations, random seeds), and well-designed synthetic benchmark with disjoint color constraint

Strong empirical results showing geometric metrics completely fail (r≈0.11) while JER strongly predicts binding (r=0.69, p<0.0001); combined model achieves R²=0.78; findings validate on natural images (SugarCrepe, r=0.69)
Provides mechanistic insights through layer-wise JER tracking, singular value analysis, and qualitative failure cases that reveal where and why functional rank collapses

Rigorous theoretical analysis (Section 6) explaining how different training objectives constrain Jacobian structure, with detailed mathematical derivations connecting objective design to functional sensitivity
Excellent presentation with clear writing, well-designed figures that build intuition, and comprehensive appendices enabling reproducibility and verification of results
weaknesses: Limited scope of compositional evaluation: restricted primarily to synthetic geometric primitive tasks; SugarCrepe validation covers only 13 CLIP variants and 7 attribute types; unclear generalization to other forms of compositionality (part-whole hierarchies, spatial reasoning beyond left-right)

Primarily diagnostic rather than prescriptive: identifies a problem but proposes no solutions; lacks guidance on practical implications such as whether practitioners should optimize for JER during training or how this would impact downstream performance

Causal mechanism underspecified: paper shows JER correlates with binding but doesn't rigorously explain why high effective rank specifically enables compositional binding; lacks mechanistic ablations isolating which aspects of JER matter

Statistical concerns with modest sample sizes: n=26 for primary correlations with only 3-6 models per objective family; leave-one-out CV with small samples risks optimism; multiple comparisons without correction; SugarCrepe analysis (n=13, r=0.69, p=0.009) is borderline significant

Incomplete comparisons: no systematic comparison to alternative local sensitivity measures (Lipschitz constants, condition numbers); no ablation exploring whether other input-output statistics could work equally well; why JER specifically?
